 Hymenophyton flabellatum Hymenophytaceae                                         TVN
This is one of the commonest bryophytes in wet forest, rainforest and fi;rn gullies. It
forms dense colonies of umbrella-like shoots on living and fallen trees and
tree­ferns, and on rocks in streams. It is espec(ally common close to streams. The
colour is always a pure green, and the vertical stem gives way to a near-perfect circle
of forked horizontal lobes, each with a distinct midrib. The margins of the lobes are
not toothed, unlike th_ose of Symphyogyna podaphylla. Botanists unfamiliar with
liverworts might mistake the shoots for filmy ferns, with which they are often mixed.
   . H. leptopodum (T) is distinguished by its notched frond-tips.

Similar species: P;llavicinia spp., Symphyogyna podophylla, Podomitrium spp.




Lunuiaria cruciata Lunulariaceae                                                 WSTVAN
This species is extremely common on recently disturbed soil and in waste places,
urban gardens and flower-pots. It is probably the most common liverwort world-wide.
Its natural habitat is bare soil on stream banks and moist soil that dries out periodically.
It is usually distinguishable by the presence on the upper surface of crescent-shaped
gemmae j.:ups in which yellow-green, pointed-oval gemmae form. The flat thallus is
divide� into broad lobes and is dotted with whitish pores that lead to air chambers
below. Sporophytes, which are rare, each consist of a stalk supporting four capsules
arranged in a cross (hence cruciata).

Similar species: Marcha�tia spp.

Marchand'il Marchantiaceae
This genus of large thallose liverworts is well known to horticulturalists, because
the species thrive in gardens and greenhouses. Only Lunularia cruciata can be
confused with the following species, and then only when gemmae cups are absent.
The other obvious characteristic is the pres_ence of polygonal zones on the upper
surface of the thallus, each zone having a central pore leading to an air-chamber
below. The gemmae cups are circular and crown-like. The archegoniophore is also
characteristic, producing radial rows of pendent yellow capsules alternating with
sterile photosynthetic rays.

M. berteroana                                                                    WSTVAN
This species is common in grassy bogs, but is also found on the banks of streams and
other damp places. The dorsal surface is a shiny pale green and, characteristically, the
v�ntral surface is covered by pale, almost transparent scales which extend
more-or­less to the margins. Gemmae cups are usually present, except in very humid
habitats. They have toothed and slightly hairy margins, and the gemmae within
are bright green arid discus-shaped.
M. foliacea                                                                          TVAN
This is often confused with M berteroana, but the ventral scales are crimson and are
restricted to a narrow strip close to the centreline of the ventral surface of the thallus.
The archegoniophore is flat, so that the head looks like an indented disc.
WIKIPEDIA  (1) 
Hymenophyton flabellatum is a species of the order Pallaviciniales (liverworts), one of perhaps several species in the genus Hymenophyton. It is a dendroid thalloid liverwort belongs to the family Hymenophytaceae and is commonly known as Fan liverwort. It is found in New Zealand, Chile, and common in wet forests of Australia and Tasmania. Hymenophyton flabellatum closely resembles with small filmy fern, Hymenophyllum and can be confused with the liverwort, Symphyogyna hymenophyllum.
